## Overview

Ingrian Finns are the Finnish population native to Ingria, a historical region corresponding to the central part of today’s Leningrad Oblast in Russia. They originated from Lutheran Finnish settlers who moved there in the 17th century, when Finland and Ingria belonged to the Swedish Empire. Today, they constitute the largest part of the Finnish population of the Russian Federation. Some 25,000 Ingrian Finns have returned or still reside in the region of Saint Petersburg, according to some records. The sources describe a population shaped by migration, religious change, forced deportation, collectivization, Russification and dispersal across the Soviet Union. They identify Finnish and Finnish-language institutions, Lutheranism, schools, newspapers, libraries, choirs and song festivals as important parts of Ingrian Finnish cultural life.

## Material culture

### Architecture

They do record Lutheran parsonages as important cultural centers and the establishment of Finnish-language schools, but provide no architectural account of these buildings.

## Music & performance

The sources identify choirs, song festivals and the musical activity of Finnish-language cultural institutions. The first song festival in Ingria was held in Puutosti (Skuoritsa) in 1899. Lutheran parsonages served as cultural centers, while the Kolppana teachers’ and cantors’ seminary, founded in 1863, trained teachers and cantors and helped form the Ingrian intelligentsia.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources mention the first song festival in Ingria, held in Puutosti (Skuoritsa) in 1899. The sources do describe major historical processes that affected community life: the Lutheran settlement of Ingria during Swedish rule, the founding of Saint Petersburg in 1703, the abolition of serfdom in 1861, deportations during 1929–1931 and 1935–1936, and the forced relocation of most Ingrian Finns remaining in Ingria to Siberia in 1942.

## Oral tradition & literature

They do record a substantial Finnish-language institutional culture. The first Finnish-language newspaper in Ingria, Pietarin Sanomat, began publication in 1870; the first public library opened in Tyrö in 1850; and the largest library, in Skuoritsa, held over 2,000 books in the latter half of the 19th century. Finnish-language schools and the Kolppana seminary operated freely until the 1890s, when the school system began to be Russified.

## Language & religion

Ingrian Finns are Finnish people associated with Ingria and Finnish-language institutions. The settlers included the Äyrämöiset from the Karelian Isthmus, especially from Äyräpää, and the Savakot from Savo and other parts of Finland. Finnish was the official language of the Kuivaisi National District from 1928 to 1939, whose center was in Toksova. Ingrian Finns were originally Lutheran settlers, and under Russian rule they were permitted to continue practicing Lutheranism while Orthodox Christianity became dominant in the region. Many Ingrian Finns in Russia are members of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Ingria, which was historically closely associated with the community. The sources also state that many Ingrian Finns who moved to Finland spoke only Russian and in many cases continued to identify as Russians.
